title: Haemorrhagic shock: trauma team leader
stem: Resus 1. A trauma call is coming in: a 17-year-old girl, front-seat passenger in a car hit on her side at speed. Seatbelt mark across the abdomen. Ambulance: HR 128, BP 88/50, RR 24, SpO2 97%, GCS 15. You are the trauma team leader; Nurse Cheng and Dr Ng are with you. Lead the resuscitation.

phases.title: Pre-brief
phases.goal: Before she arrives: trauma call, introductions, roles, PPE, expectations, blood and ultrasound ready, how the team will talk.

phases.title: Handover and monitoring
phases.goal: A hands-off ATMIST handover; monitoring and oxygen on.

phases.title: Primary survey
phases.goal: xABCDE, each finding called out: where is she bleeding?

phases.title: Resuscitate
phases.goal: Access and bloods, the massive transfusion protocol, tranexamic acid, analgesia.

phases.title: Damage control resuscitation
phases.goal: Name it; permissive hypotension and its head-injury exception; bridge with small warmed boluses; when the blood arrives, haemostatic resuscitation and the lethal triad; reassess.

phases.title: Adjuncts and decision
phases.goal: eFAST and films; reassess; refer for damage control laparotomy.

events.say: The O-negative blood has arrived in the bay.

review.text: Initial fluid. Your notes give a 1–2 L crystalloid bolus. ATLS now limits crystalloid to 1 L at most and moves early to blood in a balanced ratio. While blood is coming, give warmed 250 mL boluses only to keep a radial pulse and mentation, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol early.

Permissive hypotension and its exception. Aim for a systolic of 80–90 mmHg until the bleeding is controlled, except in traumatic brain injury: there keep systolic at least 110 mmHg (ages 15–49 and over 70) or at least 100 mmHg (ages 50–69).
Shock classes. ATLS 10th added base deficit to the table: class II −2 to −6, class III −6 to −10, class IV below −10 mmol/L.
ATLS 11th edition specifics (xABCDE as the order) are quoted from memory; I could not check the manual here.

No HA massive transfusion protocol document was available: the script says 'activate the massive transfusion protocol' without HA pack contents or activation numbers. Add your hospital's if you want them said.

notes:
Checked against ATLS 11th edition (xABCDE, shock classes with base deficit), NICE NG39 (major trauma, 2016, reviewed), CRASH-2, and RCEM trauma team leader guidance.

Your notes cover this scenario well. Differences:
• Initial fluid: your notes say a 1–2 L crystalloid bolus. ATLS now limits crystalloid to 1 L at most and moves early to blood in a balanced ratio; NICE advises blood products, not crystalloid, in active bleeding.
• While blood is on its way: do not withhold volume from a crashing patient, and do not flood her either. Give warmed crystalloid in 250 mL boluses, reassessing after each, only to keep a radial pulse and mentation, then switch to blood the moment it arrives. Activate the major haemorrhage protocol early so the wait is short.
• PERMISSIVE HYPOTENSION: aim for a systolic of 80–90 mmHg (palpable radial pulse, talking) until the bleeding is controlled. A higher pressure pops clots and more fluid dilutes clotting factors.
• EXCEPTION — TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY: no permissive hypotension. Hypotension roughly doubles mortality after TBI. Keep systolic ≥110 mmHg (aged 15–49 or over 70) or ≥100 mmHg (aged 50–69), MAP ≥80 (ATLS 10th–11th, Brain Trauma Foundation). In combined bleeding and head injury, give blood (and crystalloid while waiting) to hold that pressure, and control the bleeding fast.
• Vasopressors are not a substitute for volume in haemorrhagic shock.
• Shock classes: ATLS 10th added base deficit (class II −2 to −6, class III −6 to −10, class IV below −10). Heart-rate cut-offs in your table are close enough.
• TXA: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours, within 3 hours — as in your notes.

A seatbelt sign raises the risk of hollow viscus, mesenteric and lumbar spine (Chance) injuries. A positive FAST in an unstable patient means laparotomy; stable or responding patients can have CT. Ask for a pregnancy test in any female of reproductive age.

Team leader behaviours scored: pre-brief, roles, closed-loop communication, summarising aloud, and deciding on disposition.

Perfect script and its key words were checked against four independent mark schemes (HKCEM-style, RCEM team leader, ATLS checklist, and a keyword-based scheme). Added from that check: damage control resuscitation and haemostatic resuscitation named; the lethal triad and calcium (European guideline on management of major bleeding after trauma, 2023: monitor and maintain ionised calcium during massive transfusion); crystalloid limited to 1 L; warmer/rapid infuser; oxygen; closed-loop and hands-off leadership; reassessment as a transient responder; SBAR referral for damage control laparotomy; theatre, anaesthesia and ICU; secondary and tertiary surveys; the Chance fracture risk; family and documentation.

Bedside checks (pulse, ABCDE, reassessment) are done at the patient, with close-ups, not said to the nurse.

Audit: the response to the bridging bolus is found at the patient, not reported by the nurse.

steps.label: Pre-brief the team
steps.hint: Trauma call; introductions, I lead; roles; PPE; what we expect; blood, warmer and ultrasound; closed-loop.

opts.t: Please put out a full trauma team activation.
opts.mark: Activates the trauma team

opts.t: Hello everyone, I'm the emergency physician and the trauma team leader; I'll stay hands-off. Names and experience, please.
opts.mark: Introduces the team and declares the team leader

opts.t: Roles: Dr Ng, airway and cervical spine. Nurse Cheng, IV access, bloods and drugs. Could someone scribe and record the times.
opts.mark: Allocates roles, including a scribe

opts.t: Everyone in full PPE, please.
opts.mark: Team PPE

opts.t: Our shared mental model: a 17-year-old, side impact, seatbelt sign, hypotensive. I expect intra-abdominal haemorrhage, most likely the spleen.
opts.mark: Shares the expected injury (shared mental model)

opts.t: Please have O-negative blood, a fluid warmer or rapid infuser and the ultrasound for an eFAST ready, and warn the blood bank.
opts.mark: Prepares blood, warmer and ultrasound; warns the blood bank

opts.t: We'll use closed-loop communication: repeat back each instruction. I'll summarise at intervals.
opts.mark: Sets closed-loop communication

steps.label: Paramedic handover
steps.hint: Hands-off handover (ATMIST): age, time, mechanism, injuries, signs, treatment.

ATMIST.t: Age, and the time of injury?

ATMIST.r: Side impact on her side at about 70 km/h, belted, airbags deployed. Car door intruded.
Seatbelt bruise across the lower abdomen, tender left upper quadrant. Left chest wall sore.
Oxygen, 18 G right arm, 250 mL saline, collar.

steps.label: Monitoring and oxygen
steps.hint: Monitor, oxygen; transfer with spinal precautions.

opts.t: Monitoring on, please: ECG, blood pressure every 3 minutes and SpO2.
opts.mark: Puts her on continuous monitoring

opts.t: High-flow oxygen, 15 litres via a non-rebreather.
opts.mark: Gives high-flow oxygen

steps.label: Primary survey
steps.hint: xABCDE: say each finding out loud for the scribe.

x A B.mark: Checks for catastrophic external haemorrhage first

x A B.r: Talking, airway patent. "Airway patent; maintain spinal motion restriction."
RR 24, trachea central, equal air entry, tender left lower ribs. "Possible left rib fractures; no tension pneumothorax or massive haemothorax."
x A B.mark: Breathing: excludes tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax

C.r: HR 128, BP 88/50, cool, CRT 4 s, anxious. "This is class III haemorrhagic shock: about 30 to 40 percent of her blood volume."
Seatbelt sign; tender and guarding in the left upper quadrant; left shoulder-tip pain. "Kehr's sign: likely splenic injury."
C.mark: Abdomen: left upper quadrant signs and Kehr's sign

C.r: Pelvis not tender to gentle pressure (not sprung); femurs normal. "Not the pelvis or the long bones."
C.mark: Looks for the other sources: pelvis and long bones

D E.r: GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, glucose 6.5. "No evidence of a head injury."
D E.mark: Disability: GCS, pupils and glucose; no head injury

D E.r: No other injuries. Temperature 36.1. Warm blankets on. "Keep her warm."

steps.label: Resuscitate
steps.hint: Two large-bore cannulae and bloods (crossmatch, gas, calcium, pregnancy test); the massive transfusion protocol.

opts.t: Nurse Cheng: two large-bore cannulae; bloods for FBC, clotting, crossmatch, a venous gas with lactate and base deficit, ionised calcium, and a pregnancy test.
opts.mark: Two large-bore cannulae; bloods with crossmatch, gas, calcium and pregnancy test
opts.r: Nurse Cheng: Done. Gas: pH 7.26, base deficit −8, lactate 4.6, Hb 96, ionised calcium 1.08. hCG negative.

opts.t: Please activate the massive transfusion protocol now.
opts.mark: Activates the massive transfusion protocol early
opts.r: Nurse Cheng: Massive transfusion protocol activated. O-negative is 10 minutes away. BP 80/46 now.

steps.label: Drug cart
steps.hint: Tranexamic acid within 3 hours; titrated analgesia.

opts.mark: Gives tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours of injury
opts.t: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours
opts.dose: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours

opts.mark: Titrated IV analgesia
opts.t: Fentanyl 25–50 microgram IV, titrated

steps.label: Damage control resuscitation
steps.hint: Say it: damage control resuscitation; permissive hypotension 80–90; the head-injury exception.

opts.t: This is damage control resuscitation: permissive hypotension, haemostatic resuscitation and early haemorrhage control.
opts.mark: Names damage control resuscitation and its parts

opts.t: Permissive hypotension: we're aiming for a systolic of 80 to 90, a radial pulse and her talking, until the bleeding is controlled.
opts.mark: Permissive hypotension: systolic 80–90 until haemorrhage control

opts.t: There's no head injury; if there were, I'd keep the systolic at 110 or more.
opts.mark: States the head-injury exception

steps.label: Drug cart
steps.hint: While the blood comes: warmed 250 mL boluses only to a radial pulse; crystalloid 1 L at most.

opts.mark: Bridges with warmed 250 mL boluses, crystalloid 1 L at most
opts.t: Warmed crystalloid 250 mL bolus, then reassess (1 L at most)
opts.dose: 250 mL bolus, then reassess (1 L at most)

steps.label: Blood has arrived
steps.hint: Haemostatic resuscitation 1:1:1 through the warmer; prevent the lethal triad, calcium; reassess.

opts.t: The O-negative is here: haemostatic resuscitation, 1:1:1 plasma, platelets and red cells, through the warmer.
opts.early: The blood is not here yet.
opts.mark: Haemostatic resuscitation: balanced 1:1:1 through a warmer
opts.r: Nurse Cheng: Blood running through the warmer.

opts.t: Prevent the lethal triad: keep her warm, restore perfusion against the acidosis, and give calcium during transfusion.
opts.mark: Prevents the lethal triad and replaces calcium

steps.label: Reassess her
steps.hint: After the bolus and after each unit: pulse, pressure, refill.

After each unit.t: Reassess after the bolus: radial pulse, conscious level, pressure
After each unit.r: Radial pulse back; she's answering. BP 86/50. "Responding for now: no more crystalloid; blood next."

After each unit.t: Reassess after each unit: pulse, blood pressure, refill
After each unit.early: Give the blood first, then reassess.
After each unit.r: After 2 units BP came up to 98/60, now drifting back to 84/50, HR 124. "She is a transient responder."

steps.label: Adjuncts
steps.hint: eFAST, chest and pelvic films in the bay.

Bedside.r: Free fluid in Morison's pouch and the splenorenal space; no pericardial fluid; lung sliding both sides. "eFAST positive."
Left lower rib fractures, no pneumothorax, no haemothorax.

steps.label: Phone
steps.hint: SBAR to the surgeon: unstable, eFAST positive, transient responder: damage control laparotomy. Theatre, anaesthesia, ICU.

opts.t: Surgeon, this is the trauma team leader. A 17-year-old, side-impact crash, in class III haemorrhagic shock; eFAST positive, transient responder after 2 units and TXA. Please come now for an emergency damage control laparotomy.
opts.mark: SBAR referral for damage control laparotomy

opts.t: Please alert theatre, the anaesthetist and ICU.
opts.mark: Mobilises theatre, anaesthesia and ICU
opts.r: Theatre is being prepared; the anaesthetist is on the way.

steps.label: Summarise and hand over
steps.ask: The surgeon has arrived. Summarise for the team and hand over.
steps.hint: Summarise aloud; the plan after theatre; spinal care; family; documentation.

opts.t: Summary for the team: 17-year-old, side impact, class III haemorrhagic shock, eFAST positive, left rib fractures, transient responder after 2 units and TXA, going for damage control laparotomy.
opts.mark: Summarises aloud and hands over

opts.t: Secondary survey once the bleeding is controlled, and a tertiary survey later. Spinal precautions continue: the seatbelt sign raises the risk of a Chance fracture and bowel injury.
opts.mark: Plans the secondary and tertiary survey; spinal precautions

opts.t: I'll update her family, and the scribe's record has the time of every drug and unit.
opts.mark: Informs the family; documentation with times

qs.a: Permissive hypotension, haemostatic resuscitation and early haemorrhage control
wrong: Aggressive crystalloid to a normal pressure, then early CT and surgery
Vasopressors to a normal pressure, with plasma given only after the CT
Two litres of warmed crystalloid, then blood once the CT has been reported

qs.q: Class III haemorrhage (ATLS) means blood loss of…
Base deficit in class III shock?
What does FAST not reliably detect?
A seatbelt sign raises concern for…
qs.a: Bowel, mesentery and lumbar spine injury
wrong: Skin bruising only, which is benign
An isolated open-book pelvic ring fracture
A head injury from the steering wheel

qs.q: Target systolic before haemorrhage control, without a head injury?
qs.why: Permissive hypotension limits clot disruption and dilution until the bleeding is controlled.

qs.q: Why no permissive hypotension with a traumatic brain injury?
qs.a: Low pressure cuts cerebral perfusion and worsens secondary injury
wrong: Blood transfusion is not used in head injury
The injured brain autoregulates at any pressure
qs.why: Keep systolic ≥110 (≥100 if aged 50–69) and MAP ≥80.

qs.q: Positive FAST in an unresponsive shocked patient: next?

rules.fail: No pre-brief before she arrived: roles and expectations should be set first.

badge.name: Team Leader
badge.flavor: Brief, lead, summarise. Blood, not saline. FAST positive and unstable: theatre.

cards.q: Permissive hypotension target in bleeding trauma without a head injury?
cards.why: Until the bleeding is controlled. Not in traumatic brain injury.

cards.q: Bleeding trauma with a traumatic brain injury: blood pressure target?
options: Systolic 80–90 mmHg, as for any bleeding
No target until the CT is done
cards.why: Hypotension roughly doubles mortality after TBI.

cards.q: Bleeding trauma patient, blood 10 minutes away, peri-arrest. Fluid now?
options: Warmed 250 mL crystalloid boluses to a radial pulse
Nothing at all until the blood arrives
2 L of saline wide open, then reassess
cards.why: Bridge with small boluses; switch to blood as soon as it arrives.

cards.q: ATLS class II haemorrhage blood loss?
cards.why: Class II: tachycardia, normal systolic, narrowed pulse pressure, base deficit −2 to −6.

cards.q: Which parameter did ATLS add to the shock classes?
cards.why: Base deficit correlates with blood loss and transfusion need.

options: Left shoulder-tip pain from splenic bleeding
Right iliac fossa pain on pressing the left side

cards.q: Unstable trauma patient with a positive FAST: disposition?
cards.why: Unstable patients do not go to CT.

cards.q: Which behaviour is NOT expected of a trauma team leader?
options: Allocating roles before the patient arrives
cards.why: The leader stays hands-off to keep oversight.

cards.q: Why test for pregnancy in every female trauma patient of reproductive age?
options: It changes imaging, drugs and obstetric input
It predicts splenic injury after blunt trauma
It is required before a FAST scan
A positive test excludes hypovolaemic shock

cards.q: The 'lethal diamond' adds which to the lethal triad?
cards.why: Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypocalcaemia (citrate in transfused blood binds calcium).
cards.source: European guideline on bleeding after trauma (2023)

script.say: Hello everyone, I'm Dr __, the emergency physician. I'll be the trauma team leader and I'll stay hands-off. Could we go round with names and experience?
Please put out a full trauma team activation.
Roles: Dr Ng, airway and cervical spine. Nurse Cheng, IV access, bloods and drugs. Could someone scribe and record the times. Everyone in full PPE, please.

Our shared mental model: we're expecting a 17-year-old girl from a side-impact crash with a seatbelt sign and hypotension. My main concern is intra-abdominal haemorrhage, most likely the spleen. Please have O-negative blood, a fluid warmer or rapid infuser and the ultrasound for an eFAST ready, and warn the blood bank.
We'll use closed-loop communication: please repeat back each instruction. I'll summarise at intervals.
Paramedic, a hands-off handover please: ATMIST.
script.do: Age 17; injured 25 minutes ago; side impact at 70 km/h, belted, door intrusion; seatbelt bruise, left upper quadrant and left chest pain; HR 110 to 128, BP 104/70 to 88/50; oxygen, one cannula, 250 mL saline, collar.

script.say: Monitoring on: ECG, blood pressure every 3 minutes and SpO2. High-flow oxygen, 15 litres via a non-rebreather.
Primary survey, xABCDE. No catastrophic external haemorrhage. Airway patent, she's talking; maintain spinal motion restriction.
script.do: Look at the airway; talk to her.

script.say: Breathing: respiratory rate 24, trachea central, equal air entry, tender left lower ribs. Possible rib fractures; no tension pneumothorax or massive haemothorax.
script.do: Look, feel, percuss and listen to the chest.

script.say: Circulation: heart rate 128, BP 88/50, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds and anxious. This is class III haemorrhagic shock, about 30 to 40 percent of her blood volume.

Sources of bleeding: chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones and the floor. Seatbelt sign, left upper quadrant tenderness and guarding, and left shoulder-tip pain: Kehr's sign, likely a splenic injury. Pelvis not tender; I won't spring it. Long bones normal.
script.do: Palpate the abdomen; gentle pressure on the pelvis; the femurs.

script.say: Nurse Cheng: two large-bore cannulae; bloods for FBC, clotting, crossmatch, a venous gas with lactate and base deficit, ionised calcium, and a pregnancy test. Please activate the massive transfusion protocol now.
script.do: Gas: pH 7.26, base deficit −8, lactate 4.6; hCG negative. Blood 10 minutes away; BP 80/46.

script.say: Tranexamic acid 1 gram IV over 10 minutes now, within 3 hours of injury, then 1 gram over 8 hours. Fentanyl 25 to 50 micrograms IV, titrated, for pain.
Disability: GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, glucose 6.5. No evidence of a head injury. Exposure: no other injuries; temperature 36.1; warm blankets on.
script.do: GCS, pupils, glucose; expose fully, then cover.

script.say: This is damage control resuscitation: permissive hypotension, haemostatic resuscitation and early haemorrhage control.

Permissive hypotension: we're aiming for a systolic of 80 to 90, a radial pulse and her talking, until the bleeding is controlled. There's no head injury; if there were, I'd keep the systolic at 110 or more.
Until the blood arrives, warmed crystalloid in 250 mL boluses, reassessing after each, and no more than a litre in total.
script.do: 250 mL in: radial pulse back, BP 86/50.

script.say: The O-negative is here: haemostatic resuscitation, 1:1:1 plasma, platelets and red cells, through the warmer. Prevent the lethal triad: keep her warm, restore perfusion against the acidosis, and give calcium during transfusion.
eFAST please, and a chest and pelvic X-ray in the bay.
script.do: eFAST: free fluid in Morison's pouch and the splenorenal space; no pericardial fluid. Chest: left lower rib fractures, no pneumothorax. Pelvis: normal.

script.say: Reassessing after 2 units: the pressure came up to 98/60 and is drifting back to 84/50. She is a transient responder with a positive eFAST: she needs a laparotomy, not a CT.

Surgeon, this is Dr __, trauma team leader. A 17-year-old, side-impact crash, in class III haemorrhagic shock. eFAST positive with left upper quadrant signs and left rib fractures. Massive transfusion protocol running, TXA given, transient responder after 2 units. Please come now for an emergency damage control laparotomy.
Please alert theatre, the anaesthetist and ICU.
Summary for the team: 17-year-old, side impact, class III haemorrhagic shock, eFAST positive, left rib fractures, transient responder after 2 units and TXA, going for damage control laparotomy.
Secondary survey once the bleeding is controlled, and a tertiary survey later. Spinal precautions continue: the seatbelt sign raises the risk of a Chance fracture and bowel or mesenteric injury.
I'll update her family, and the scribe's record has the time of every drug and unit.
